items_missed: Opened with the wrong name. 'Nick, good afternoon. This is Cameron with Einstein Moving Company' — the customer had to correct him with 'Yes, this is Devonte.' He recovered fine, but the first thing this customer heard was his own name wrong.
Never asked 'how are you today?' or ran any warm-up at all — straight from the wrong name into 'you were trying to get a move done tomorrow.'

No agenda statement. 'If you'd like, I can go over all the details move and see if it would be possible in the afternoon' is a permission ask, not a roadmap — no sequence, no timeframe, no 'sound good?'

Stairs and floors never asked at either end. He is moving a 200-gallon glass aquarium and a stand and never established whether either address has a step in it. Stairs are the single biggest time and risk variable on a heavy fragile item and the question was never put.

Special considerations never probed — no doorway widths, no narrow hallways, no tight turns. A 200-gallon tank is roughly six feet long and does not pivot; whether it clears a turn is the question that decides if this job happens at all, and it was never asked.
Access never probed — no parking, no elevator, no gate, no loading area at either address.
Moving-stressor question never asked.

Never asked whether the tank would be drained and emptied before move day. Not a scored rubric bullet, but it is the operational fact the whole booking rests on — a full 200-gallon tank is roughly 1,700 pounds and cannot be moved at all. He accepted '£300 or so' as the weight of the glass and moved on.
No 'pricing is super simple' opener — he used 'to jump straight to the point,' which is efficient but skips the frame.

What's-included list never given. 'We don't charge dollar more not for taxes, not for insurance, not for anything at all. All that's included' covers the concept but never names the truck, the blankets, the shrink wrap, the dollies or the tools — so the customer does not know what actually arrives.
Disassembly/reassembly never mentioned, on a job whose second item is literally a stand that has to come apart from a tank.
Meet Your Mover never mentioned.

On-Time Guarantee never mentioned — and this is the costliest miss on the call, because he sold a floating arrival time instead: 'looks like earliest availability we have a truck that's first job is scheduled to end at 12:30. So, I would throw you on the schedule here for about 1:30 PM,' followed by 'the lead from that job will also be keeping in contact with you towards the end of their first job. Let you know whether or not it'd be going a little faster... or you know running a little longer.' He told a next-day customer the window may slip and then did not attach the guarantee that makes that acceptable.
Clock start never explained — nothing about the clock starting on-site when the contract opens.

Fifteen-minute proration never mentioned. He stated the 2.5-hour minimum three times and never said what happens past it, which on a minimum-priced booking is exactly the number the customer will care about on move day.

No typical time range for this job — he gave a single point ('that should only be our minimum') with no band around it. If the tank takes three hours instead of two and a half, the customer has been given no warning that the number can move.
Truck count never stated, and the mover count only came out because the customer asked: 'How many people would that be? Is it like two to 34?'
Walk distance never asked at either end.
No equivalents or plain-language anchors used anywhere.

Prep speech absent. The consolidation and carload bullets are genuinely N/A on a two-item partial move and are granted, but the core 'prep before move day means a shorter move and a lower bill' line still applied and was never said — draining the tank, clearing the stand and opening the path is exactly that speech in this job's language.

BOLDED-details framing and the 'reply with any corrections' ask both absent. He did verify the email and both addresses out loud, which is better than most of this batch, but never asked the customer to check the written confirmation.
Hours and how to reach us never given, on a move happening the very next day.
Customer's name used once, correctly, after opening with the wrong one — short of the 3+ standard.
top_strength: Two things stand out, and the first is the rate explanation, which is the cleanest per-mover-per-hour framing in the entire batch. When the customer asked how many people he was getting, Cameron did not just answer the question — he rebuilt the whole number in front of him: 'That's for two guys to, to explain the pricing a little, a little better. So, we charge $97 per hour per mover. So with our stand through to two mover team that'd be $194 per hour. And then, if we're just moving that, I guess those two pieces for you then that should only be our minimum. Which is gonna be a two and a half.' That is the rubric's exact structure — rate per mover, crew size, combined hourly, then the minimum — delivered unprompted in response to a different question. Most reps in this batch quote a blended hourly and let the customer wonder where it came from. The second is the insurance answer, which is the best on any of the eight calls this week. The customer asked a soft version of the question — 'And you said like insurance and stuff that's already included to the price and stuff' — and Cameron gave him the full comparison: 'the insurance is, is included. We use or I guess we set aside $2,000 per move to a fair replace or reimburse for any external damages. So we go away above and beyond that 60¢ per pound state requirement.' The $2,000, the repair/replace/reimburse mechanism, and the 60-cents-per-pound industry baseline all landed in one answer. He is the only rep this week to give the customer the contrast that makes the coverage mean anything. Worth noting he is also the only one who thought to name the mechanism as a set-aside rather than as vague 'insurance.' Third, he volunteered the whole low-friction commercial block without being asked: 'we don't require, we don't require a deposit nor is there any cancellation fee. They don't actually take any of your credit card information till after the move is all set and done.' No deposit, no cancellation fee, and no card up front — three reasons to say yes today, delivered proactively to a customer who was already leaning in. That combination is why this call booked in six minutes.
coaching_note: First, the good news: this booked, next-day, in six minutes, and the customer closed with 'Awesome, appreciate you man.' Cameron's commercial instincts are strong and the no-deposit / no-cancellation-fee / card-after-the-move block plus the 60-cents-per-pound insurance contrast are the best-delivered content in this week's sample. The problem is what he booked. Highest-leverage fix by a wide margin: he committed a truck to a 200-gallon glass aquarium without asking a single qualifying question. No stairs at either end, no doorway or hallway width, no tight turns, no parking, no walk distance — and critically, never asked whether the tank will be drained and empty when the crew arrives. He accepted the customer's '£300 or so' for the glass and priced it at the bare 2.5-hour minimum. A full 200-gallon tank is roughly 1,700 pounds of water and cannot be moved by anyone; an empty one still does not turn corners. This is a crew that can arrive tomorrow at 1:30 to a job that is either impossible or a two-hour problem, and neither outcome is recoverable at that point. The rule to install: any specialty item over roughly 200 pounds gets four questions before a number is given — is it empty, how does it get out of the room, how does it get into the truck, and how does it get in at the other end. Second priority: the On-Time Guarantee, which he needed more than any other rep this week and never said. He sold a soft window — 'first job is scheduled to end at 12:30. So, I would throw you on the schedule here for about 1:30' — and then warned the customer it might slip. That is a customer sitting at home tomorrow afternoon with no commitment from us. The line is: 'And if we miss that window, we start discounting your bill immediately — that's on us, not you.' It costs nothing to say and it converts a soft window into a promise. Third, the clock is half-covered. He stated the 2.5-hour minimum three separate times and never once said what happens after it. On a job priced at exactly the minimum, the fifteen-minute proration is the number most likely to appear on the final bill, and the customer has never heard it. Add 'and if we go past two and a half hours, we prorate in fifteen-minute increments from there — so you only pay for what you actually use.' Estimate-accuracy flag for the bottom-4 review, and note this one runs the opposite direction from the usual pattern: Cameron under-quoted rather than padded. He gave a single point estimate at the floor — 'that should only be our minimum' — with no range, no stairs information, and no access information. Amanda's known failure pattern is managers padding conservatively on large homes and underestimating apartments; this is a third variant worth watching, which is quoting the minimum on a specialty-item job because the item count is low. Item count is not the driver on a 200-gallon tank; handling is. Worth pulling the actual on this one when it closes — if it runs past 2.5 hours, that is a customer who was told $485 next-day and billed more, on a move he agreed to in under a minute. Last, fix the delivery of numbers. The transcript has him saying 'So, how we get to $45?' and 'A 300 gallon fifteen that's... Alright, $300.50' — if any of that is what the customer actually heard, a booked job just went out with the wrong price attached to it.
phone_presence_notes: Easy, confident and likeable — steady 'Yes sir,' a willingness to rebuild the pricing math when the customer asked rather than repeating himself, and unprompted reassurance about the deposit and the card, all of which earned a genuine 'Awesome, appreciate you man' at the close; held off a 5 by opening with the wrong name, skipping any warm-up, and a delivery that garbled several of the numbers.
audio_review_reason: The money is unreadable in the transcript and it matters, because this call resulted in a confirmed next-day booking. He is transcribed saying 'So, how we get to $45?' immediately after correctly deriving $485, and 'A 300 gallon fifteen that's, that should definitely be within our. Alright, $300.50.' Audio is the only way to establish whether the customer was actually quoted $485 cleanly or whether Cameron misspoke the price on a job that is on the schedule for tomorrow at 1:30. Secondary: several of his sentences break off mid-clause in the transcript, and it is worth confirming whether that is pace and trailing-off in delivery or a line-quality artifact.
